newsitem.title: FRANCE: French fishermen end Channel blockade.
newsitem.headline: French fishermen end Channel blockade.

text.p: Fishermen lifted a blockade of French Channel ports on Thursday after the Paris government promised to raise their protest against new European Union regulations at an EU ministers meeting in June.

A spokesman for the fishermen, who earlier suspended their three-day-old blockade during the talks with Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Philippe Vasseur, said they could reimpose the blockade if their demands against fish conservation measures imposing larger mesh nets were rejected.
The fishing boat blockade of Boulogne, Calais and Dunkirk had crippled traffic to and from the three ports and stranded hundreds of trucks on both sides of the Channel.

Under a new regulation to come into force in January 1998, minimum mesh sizes for fixed nets used for catching sole will be raised to 120 mm from 80 mm. The regulation, which primarily affects French fishermen, does not cover nets towed by trawlers.
The fishermen say larger holes may cut their catch by half.
A ministry spokesman said Vasseur promised during 90-minute talks with fishermen's representatives to ask a meeting of EU fisheries ministers on June 17 to modify the regulations.
In the meantime, he ordered a report into the social and technical implications to back the fishermen's demands.
Vasseur said in a statement after meeting shipping companies that they had agreed to drop claims for compensation from the fishermen over the blockade.
"I had indicated that the State would mediate to ensure the claims are dropped. This has been agreed," Vasseur said.
A French court had ordered the fishermen on Wednesday to lift the blockade, granting an injunction to European ferry companies P&O, Stena Line AB and Sea France.
European transport commissioner Neil Kinnock called on Thursday for compensation for lorry drivers caught by French fishermen's protest, his spokeswoman said.
Near the English port of Dover, up to 400 truck drivers stranded in an 18-mile (29 km) motorway traffic jam that began on Tuesday prepared to move their vehicles.
